summary:
MARSPath is an AI-powered Martian exploration and astronaut safety platform that transforms complex NASA planetary datasets into actionable mission intelligence. Built using React, OpenLayers, Python, and FastAPI, it integrates NASA/USGS terrain imagery, MOLA and HiRISE elevation data, environmental observations, and orbital information into an interactive mission-control system.

Our geospatial engine processes elevation, slope, surface roughness, and terrain hazards to generate optimized routes using A* and Dijkstra algorithms. Beyond shortest-path navigation, MARSPath evaluates route safety, scientific waypoints, estimated traversal effort, EVA time budgets, and return-to-base feasibility.

The platform combines multi-layer risk analysis, Monte Carlo uncertainty assessment, alternative-route comparison, and AI-assisted scientific interpretation. Its astronaut-centred capabilities include a Marswalk Survivability Score, simulated suit telemetry, spoken hazard alerts, solar-storm scenario modelling, and planetary-protection geofencing. Authentic rover imagery supports contextual surface reconnaissance.

MARSPath bridges the gap between raw planetary science and operational decisions. By unifying terrain intelligence, human safety constraints, robotic exploration, and explainable risk assessment, it demonstrates how future Mars missions can plan safer traverses, respond to changing conditions, protect scientifically sensitive environments, and maximize exploration value. ,
details:
MARSPath is a Martian navigation and mission intelligence platform developed to make future exploration of Mars safer, more efficient, and scientifically productive. The idea behind the project is to go beyond conventional route planning and create a system that helps mission teams understand the terrain, evaluate environmental hazards, manage mission resources, and make informed decisions before and during a traverse. Instead of simply identifying the shortest path between two locations, MARSPath considers whether a route is actually suitable for exploration, how difficult it may be to navigate, what risks it presents, and whether astronauts can safely return within their available mission time.

We developed an interactive Mission Control platform that brings together data from NASA and other authoritative planetary science resources. It uses Mars surface imagery, elevation models, terrain observations, environmental measurements, and orbital information to build a detailed picture of the Martian landscape. Global Viking imagery, regional CTX mosaics, and high-resolution HiRISE observations provide different levels of surface detail, while MOLA and other elevation products support terrain analysis. The platform also incorporates information from NASA's Planetary Data System, THEMIS, CRISM, MEDA, and SPICE-based orbital data. Each source contributes a different perspective, from surface composition and thermal properties to atmospheric observations and spacecraft geometry. We have also focused on preserving data provenance and distinguishing measured observations from derived calculations, historical information, predictions, and simulated scenarios.

A major part of MARSPath is its geospatial analysis and route optimization engine. Using Python-based scientific computing and geospatial processing, the system analyses elevation, slope, surface roughness, and terrain hazards to determine which areas are suitable for traversal. It implements A* and Dijkstra algorithms to calculate optimized routes while considering more than just geographical distance. Routes are evaluated using terrain difficulty, weighted traversal cost, maximum slope, hazard exposure, estimated effort, and mission duration. Mission planners can compare alternative routes and choose between safety-first, balanced, and science-first objectives. Scientific waypoints can also be incorporated into a route, allowing exploration opportunities to be considered alongside operational constraints.

We extended this navigation system to address the specific challenges of human exploration through astronaut-centred EVA planning. The Marswalk Survivability Score provides a 0–100 decision-support index based on factors such as terrain safety, slope, distance, EVA duration, and return feasibility. Rather than displaying a score without explanation, MARSPath provides a breakdown of the contributing factors so that mission teams can understand why a particular route is considered more or less suitable. The Suit HUD provides an astronaut-oriented interface displaying simulated oxygen reserves, suit battery levels, mission elapsed time, remaining distance, estimated return time, and current hazard conditions. Browser-based speech functionality delivers spoken warnings when important hazards or resource thresholds are encountered, while visual alerts ensure that critical information remains accessible even when audio is unavailable. These suit values are explicitly treated as simulated demonstration telemetry rather than measurements from an actual spacesuit.

Environmental conditions can also change the feasibility of a mission. To demonstrate this, MARSPath includes a Solar Storm Scenario that models the potential impact of increased radiation risk on an EVA. Activating the scenario updates the modeled risk contribution, Marswalk Survivability Score, safety warnings, and return-safety envelope. This allows operators to compare normal and adverse environmental conditions and understand how a mission plan may need to change. The scenario is clearly identified as simulated unless supported by a verified external observation. MARSPath further uses Monte Carlo simulations, uncertainty assessment, and environmental stress scenarios to examine how variations in assumptions and conditions can affect route safety and mission outcomes.

Another important consideration is planetary protection. Scientific exploration should not compromise environments that may contain evidence of past or present Martian habitability. MARSPath therefore includes a toggleable planetary-protection geofence with a Robot-Only Buffer visualization. When a proposed route intersects a displayed sensitive zone, the platform highlights the affected area and provides a warning. The system distinguishes officially designated Special Regions from candidate sensitive areas and demonstration-only buffers, rather than treating every mineralogical indication as an officially protected boundary. This creates a practical way to consider planetary-protection constraints during route planning. We also incorporate robotic reconnaissance concepts through Scout Rover support and authentic Perseverance surface imagery within Jezero Crater waypoint popups, providing additional visual context for locations of scientific interest.

MARSPath also considers the role of orbiting spacecraft in supporting surface exploration. Its orbital intelligence capabilities use available information for missions such as Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Mars Odyssey, MAVEN, Mars Express, and ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter. The platform visualizes relevant orbital geometry and observation information and incorporates terrain-based communication awareness to identify potential radio line-of-sight obstructions. It also accounts for the significant communication delay between Earth and Mars, supporting the need for more autonomous and resilient mission operations. These capabilities help highlight situations where communication may be constrained, while keeping estimated visibility separate from verified relay availability.

To make this information easier to interpret, we developed an AI-assisted Mars Science Copilot that supports natural-language mission planning, scientific terrain interpretation, candidate-route comparison, and mission-risk briefings. It helps translate mission objectives into structured planning requests and explains the trade-offs between alternative routes using available application data. AI-generated recommendations remain advisory and do not override deterministic routing constraints or engineering safety limits. The platform also brings its analyses together through an interactive map-based Mission Control interface, where users can explore terrain layers, routes, scientific waypoints, hazard overlays, return-to-base isochrones, mission budgets, and intelligence panels. Mission results can additionally be compiled into PDF mission dossiers for documentation and review.

We built MARSPath using React, Vite, JavaScript, and OpenLayers for the frontend, with Python and FastAPI powering the backend. Its scientific and geospatial processing uses tools including NumPy, Pandas, GeoPandas, Rasterio, and SciPy, alongside pathfinding algorithms, terrain analysis, uncertainty modelling, and NASA data integrations. The AI assistance layer uses Gemini-based capabilities, while the application is deployed through Vercel for the frontend and Render for the backend.

What makes MARSPath different is the way it connects planetary science with the practical realities of exploration. A route that looks optimal on a map may expose an astronaut to difficult terrain, consume too much EVA time, cross a sensitive environment, or leave insufficient margin for a safe return. Our platform brings these considerations into the same planning workflow. Its purpose is not simply to show astronauts where they can go, but to help mission teams understand the consequences of going there. By combining NASA data, geospatial intelligence, route optimization, environmental scenario modelling, robotic reconnaissance, and human-centred safety planning, MARSPath aims to contribute to safer decision-making and more responsible exploration of the Martian surface.
